name: Bremelanotide

lead: Bremelanotide (PT-141) is a synthetic peptide related to alpha-MSH, the hormone behind tanning and pigment. The US FDA approved it in 2019, as Vyleesi, for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding spaces it comes up mainly as a libido compound, discussed alongside Melanotan-type tanning peptides, and users mention skin darkening or freckling as a side effect.

It activates several melanocortin receptors; per the US label, MC1R and MC4R binding is most relevant at therapeutic levels, and how it improves desire is unknown. MC1R sits on pigment cells, which is why pigment changes occur. No trial has tested it as an appearance treatment; published human research concerns sexual function, and forum posts describe mixed personal results.

paras: In its approved use it is a self-administered, on-demand injection used by women before anticipated activity. Off-label use among men is discussed in peptide and bodybuilding communities mainly for libido rather than appearance.

In integrated phase 3 data, nausea (40.0% vs 1.3% on placebo), flushing, headache, and injection-site reactions were the most common adverse events, and nausea was the leading reason for stopping. Blood pressure rises transiently after dosing, and the label advises against use in people at high cardiovascular risk. Focal hyperpigmentation was rare at labelled use but occurred in over a third of subjects after up to 16 consecutive daily doses. It is a prescription drug in the US, and products from research-peptide sellers are not regulated as medicines.

angle.text: PT-141 is an approved drug for low desire in premenopausal women, and some men who use melanotan-type tanning peptides mention it too. Because it activates the pigment receptor MC1R, skin darkening or freckling can occur, but that is a known side effect and no trial has studied it for appearance.

lead: Bremelanotide, also known as PT-141 and marketed as Vyleesi, is a synthetic cyclic peptide analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH) that acts as a melanocortin receptor agonist [1][2]. It was first explored by Palatin Technologies for erectile dysfunction and later developed for women, and the US FDA approved it in 2019 for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) [3][1].

Bremelanotide is not an appearance treatment. It is included in this wiki because it is a close relative of the tanning peptide Melanotan II, is activated at the same pigment-related receptor (MC1R), and is discussed in the same communities, mostly as a libido compound used off-label or sourced from gray-market peptide sellers [4][5][6]. Forum posts describe mixed personal results [7][8].

Published human research is confined to sexual function. Randomized phase 3 trials supported approval in women [1][9], and the safety record from more than 3,500 participants in 43 studies has been reviewed [10]. The label and trial reports document nausea, transient blood pressure elevation, and focal hyperpigmentation as notable effects [10][4].
infobox: Palatin Technologies; later licensed to AMAG Pharmaceuticals [1]
Acquired, generalized HSDD in premenopausal women [4]

paras: The US label indicates Vyleesi for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized HSDD that causes marked distress and is not due to a co-existing medical or psychiatric condition, relationship problems, or the effects of a medication or drug substance [4]. It is described as an on-demand therapy that the patient administers herself by subcutaneous injection, in contrast to a daily oral drug [1]. The other drug approved for the same indication is flibanserin, and the two are reviewed together in clinical overviews of HSDD [11].

subs.h: Use in men and off-label use
paras: Early development was in men. Reports from around 2003 to 2004 described rapid, dose-dependent increases in erectile activity after PT-141 in healthy men and men with erectile dysfunction, and an intranasal spray was in phase II development for erectile dysfunction [2][9][12]. Pharmacokinetic and safety studies were also carried out with subcutaneous dosing in men, including men who responded inadequately to sildenafil [13]. Bremelanotide is not approved for use in men or for erectile dysfunction [4].

Women. A phase 2 dose-finding randomized trial in premenopausal women with female sexual dysfunction was reported in 2016, and a larger phase 2 registration enrolled 612 women with sexual arousal and/or desire disorders [14][15]. Two replicate randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (known as RECONNECT; each registered with roughly 700 participants) formed the basis of approval, and their results were published in 2019 [16][17][18]. A prespecified and integrated subgroup analysis of those trials was published in 2022 [18]. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of treatments for female desire, arousal and orgasm disorders performed pooled analyses for bremelanotide alongside flibanserin and mindfulness-based therapy [19].

Safety. A 2022 review of the full development programme (43 completed studies, about 3,500 subjects) reported nausea in 40.0% versus 1.3% on placebo, flushing in 20.3% versus 1.3%, headache in 11.3% versus 1.9%, and injection-site reactions in 5.4% versus 0.5% in the integrated double-blind phase 3 data [10]. There were no deaths and few serious adverse events [10].

Men. Early-phase studies in men tested intranasal and subcutaneous PT-141 for erectile response and pharmacokinetics [2][9][13]. No study has examined bremelanotide for facial appearance, skin tone or tanning as an outcome.

Other research. Registered studies have examined bremelanotide with tirzepatide in obesity (phase 2), in diabetic kidney disease (phase 2, 16 participants), the role of MC4R in HSDD (phase 4), and drug concentrations in breast milk [20][16]. Preclinical work in female rats has examined effects on solicitation behaviour [21].

The label lists nausea, flushing, injection-site reactions, headache and vomiting as the most common adverse reactions (incidence above 4%) [4]. Nausea was the most common reason for discontinuing in the clinical programme [10].

Each dose produces a transient rise in blood pressure and fall in heart rate that usually resolves within 12 hours, and the label advises considering cardiovascular risk and says the drug is not recommended in patients at high risk of cardiovascular disease [4]. Ambulatory monitoring in trials showed small, transient but statistically significant blood pressure increases [10].

Focal hyperpigmentation, reported in the label by about 1% of patients at up to 8 doses a month and involving the face, gums and breasts, is more likely in people with darker skin and with daily dosing [4]. In the safety review, it was rare at labelled use but occurred in more than a third of subjects after up to 16 consecutive daily doses [10].
The label notes that the few pregnancies in trials are insufficient to assess risk, and that animal studies at high exposures raise the possibility of fetal harm [4].

Bremelanotide is a cyclic heptapeptide analogue of alpha-MSH [2][13]. The label describes it as a non-selective melanocortin receptor agonist with a potency order of MC1R, MC4R, MC3R, MC5R and MC2R, and states the mechanism by which it improves HSDD is unknown [4]. MC4R is thought to be important in sexual function, and neurons expressing it are widespread in the central nervous system [1][4]. MC1R activation on melanocytes increases melanin expression and pigmentation, which the label links to hyperpigmentation [4]. In rats and non-human primates, PT-141 produced penile erections and activated hypothalamic neurons [2].

Palatin Technologies developed PT-141 under license, initially as a nasal spray for erectile dysfunction, with a phase IIb trial in men completed in September 2003 [12]. The programme later turned to women. Palatin sponsored the phase 3 trials and out-licensed North American rights to AMAG Pharmaceuticals, which submitted the New Drug Application [1]. The FDA approved Vyleesi in 2019 [1]. The label names Cosette Pharmaceuticals as the contact for adverse reaction reports [4].

A long-running T Nation information thread on Melanotan I and II lists PT-141 and bremelanotide among the pharmaceutical names of related peptides, reflecting how the compounds are grouped in peptide forums [5].

On T Nation, men on testosterone replacement therapy or struggling with libido or erections have asked about PT-141, with some reporting that PDE5 inhibitors did not help and others describing PT-141 as inconsistent or expensive, to be reserved for special occasions [7][8]. Threads include people who bought vials from peptide sites and asked how to prepare them [6][22][23]. The wiki does not reproduce preparation or dosing instructions.

lore.intro: In peptide and TRT forums, PT-141 is discussed as a libido and erection aid sourced from research-peptide vendors, and is often mentioned next to Melanotan tanning peptides [5][7][8].

claims.claim: PT-141 can raise libido and help when PDE5 inhibitors fail
Results are "hit and miss" and it is mainly for occasional use
PT-141 belongs to the same family as Melanotan II tanning peptides
Vials from peptide sites are a way to use PT-141 without a prescription

timeline.event: Phase IIb trial of intranasal PT-141 in men with erectile dysfunction completed [12].
Palatin reports plans for phase III in erectile dysfunction; PT-141 pharmacokinetic studies in men published [12][9][13].
Two phase 3 trials in premenopausal women with HSDD begin [16][17].
FDA approves bremelanotide (Vyleesi) for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized HSDD [1].
Phase 2 study of bremelanotide co-administered with tirzepatide in obesity begins [20].
